repos.desc: Leonida Is A Native PC Recompilation Of The Xbox Version Of Grand Theft Auto 6
repos.readme:
Leonida
  

Grand Theft Auto VI (Xbox Series) running natively on Windows, built on your PC from your own copy.

  Other languages |
  Status |
  How to build |
  How it works |
  Want to help? |
  Credits |
  License |
  Discord

Leonida is a static recompilation project. The Xbox Series CPU is x86-64 like a PC, so the game's code is loaded
and run natively, and the console's system software is reimplemented. The console's precompiled RDNA2 GPU programs
are translated to SPIR-V for Vulkan. The game's models, textures and audio are read from your package. All of this
happens **on your PC, from your own copy of the game**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This repository **does not contain the game, keys or an executable**, and it does not explain how to get them. You
> need your own copy, with its files already readable on disk. Nothing here decrypts or works around any protection.
> Everything the build creates (the generated shaders, extracted assets, the runtime folder and your saves) comes
> from your game and stays on your PC. Never share those files.

Discord: https://discord.gg/rexed

**Early. The game does not boot yet.** Everything that can be done without the game's executable is in place, so
work on booting can start as soon as one is available to a developer.

All 26,503 passed `spirv-val` in the [LLVM 23.1.5 Linux run at `c432cdc`](https://github.com/ItsNotRexed/Leonida/issues/644#issuecomment-7072972586). rust-anything

Rewrite your app in Rust, and prove it still behaves the same.
Point it at your app: it records what the original does, your coding agent writes the Rust one piece at a time,
and every piece is checked against that recording before it moves on. It doesn't translate code; it proves the rewrite.

  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  

Install · Releases · Claude Code plugin · MCP Registry · Real-world ports · FAQ
Languages · How it works · Whole apps · Sponsors · MIT
Made in Türkiye 🇹🇷 by erKam Yaman · ❤️ Sponsor me · Sponsored by  CodeRabbit

New in 2.0: Prettier, ported to Rust. 19x faster · 15,861 of 17,224 recorded runs fully in Rust · every run byte-identical

  
  
  Prettier against its Rust port on 59 real files from ms, Fuse.js and json-server (Apple M4). Same output, byte for byte. How it was measured.

PHP and C#: unit ports, through FFI and P/Invoke.

  
    
      Record
      record runs the original on generated edge cases, semantic traps and your own inputs, and saves what it returns or throws.
    
    
      Port
      bridge generates the Rust crate and a wrapper, so callers keep the original API. You or your agent write the Rust.
    
    
      Check
      diff replays every recorded case against the Rust, and nothing ships until they all match and gate passes.
    
    
      Lift
      When replay passes with no fallback and every unit passes gate, app lift makes it a pure Rust app. The original is never touched.

repos.desc: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow: profile Python, Node or Ruby apps, port the hot functions with your coding agent, prove they behave the same.
repos.readme:
Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow.

  

  
  
  
  
  
  
  

Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of `target/`. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway.

**fast-anything** finds those functions, has your coding agent port *only them* to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible.

## Install

```sh
npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything      # or: cargo install fast-anything
```

Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain ([rustup](https://rustup.rs)).

## Use

```sh
fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py     # or: -- node app.ts / bun app.ts / deno run -A app.ts / ruby app.rb / java App.java / mvn exec:java / gradle run / go run . / php app.php / clang -O2 main.c / Rscript app.R
```

Or step by step:

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `scan -- ` | profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are |
| `port [id]` | records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + `TASK.md` |
| `verify` | release-builds the port and replays every recorded call |
| `enable` / `disable` | swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte) |
| `bench` | times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs |
| `report` | markdown + SVG card for your PR |
| `doctor` | checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents |

`--agent` takes `claude`, `codex`, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand `TASK.md` to whatever you use.

## Proof, not vibes

That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. `FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1` runs the original any t

repos.desc: Agent skill for hill-climbing local LLM serving speed (decode, speculative decoding, prefill, KV, startup, TTFT) on any hardware and quantization
repos.readme:
# inference-optimisation

An agent skill for **hill-climbing the speed of a local LLM server** on any hardware and any quantization. It covers:

- single-user and concurrent decode
- speculative decoding
- prefill
- KV cache size
- startup time and time to first token

It works under a memory cap, and every result has to survive a full-context stability check.

It encodes how we actually got these speedups. It is not a list of flags. The workflow:

1. Compute the theoretical ceiling.
2. Change one thing at a time.
3. Measure against interleaved controls.
4. Log every result, including the failures.
5. Gate on long-context retrieval.
6. Qualify a clean, pinned build before publishing.

It works with Claude Code and any agent that loads `SKILL.md`-style skills. Any model can also follow it from [`PROMPT.md`](PROMPT.md).

## What we've been able to accomplish

Results from the hill-climbs this skill was distilled from. Every number was measured on the hardware named; see the linked sources for methods and raw data.

| Hardware | Model / quant / engine | Before → after |
|---|---|---|
| **Intel Arc B390 iGPU** (laptop, 64 GB unified LPDDR5X, ~115 GB/s) | Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B, EXL3 4 bpw, SGLang XPU + MTP | Decode, 1 user: 43.6 → **53 tok/s** (median)Decode, 4 users: 84.7 → **103 tok/s**Prefill 32K: 1,037 → **1,660 tok/s**Prefill 256K: 297 → **628 tok/s** (2.1×)KV cache: 264K tokens → **4 × 256K**Startup: 113 → **43 s**Registry Lab gates: decode 28.6 → **41.0**, prefill 255 → **667** |
| **Intel Arc Pro B70** | Qwen3.8-27B, EXL3 4 bpw, vLLM + custom XPU kernels | Decode: **91.2 tok/s** at 1 user, **365** at 16 (prose, thinking on)Same card with llama.cpp Q4_K_M: 25.0Prefill 4K/32K/128K/254K: 1,654/1,434/928/650 → **2,421/2,259/1,415/911**Agent-session replay: 193 → **147 s** |
| **Intel Arc Pro B70** | Same model, SGLang + the same kernels | Decode, 1 user: **82.6 tok/s**, vs vLLM 75.7 on the same card and day |
| **RTX 3090** | Qwen3.8-27B EXL3 3 bpw + MTP | **96.2 tok/s** prose / **141.1** code, 1 user |
| **RTX 3090** | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B EXL3 3 bpw + MTP | **251.7 / 357.9 tok/s**, 1 user |
| **RTX 3090** | Flash-Next EXL3, 256K context | MTP: 45.5 → **65.6 tok/s** |

repos.readme:
# Xbox Emulator

**Running the Xbox Series X|S library on PC. A continuation of [drycheetah84/TomBox](https://github.com/drycheetah84/TomBox).**

The runtime reimplements the console's platform layer (Xbox-flavoured Direct3D 12, precompiled RDNA2 shaders, unified-memory textures, system libraries) so dumped, already-decrypted Xbox Series X|S builds run as normal Windows processes. It is not tied to any single title. This repo tracks our continuation — new titles brought up, platform calls extended, shader stages unlocked.

Uses legally obtained, already-decrypted dumps. The runtime does no key extraction or package decryption.

**Source code:** the emulator's Rust workspace is in this repo: [`crates/`](crates/), [`tools/`](tools/) and `Cargo.toml`. It contains no game files, binaries or build output.

**Contributing:** pull requests are welcome, especially console library functions still marked missing in the [library map](docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md). See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Licensed GPL-3.0-or-later (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). Releases before this change remain available under MIT OR Apache-2.0.

repos.desc: GTA VI static recompilation research for x64 Windows. Source-built EXEs run on Windows, and two translated pixel shaders match reference outputs on hardware and WARP. Full-game startup is unverified.
repos.readme:
# Xbox2Windows

Xbox2Windows researches static recompilation from Xbox Series X|S (Scarlett) to x64 Windows. It translates selected x64 machine code into C++ and selected gfx1013 shaders into desktop DXIL. The public tests build their own inputs and run without a game installation.

**Startup status.** Source-built Windows programs run from entry to process exit. The main executable was absent from the inspected package. Execution of the title's CPU code, full-game startup and frame rate remain unverified.

[Results](#current-results-and-open-work) · [Coverage chart](#instruction-coverage) · [Community and contributions](#community-and-contributions) · [Build on Windows](#first-build) · [Choose an experiment](#choose-an-experiment) · [Run the GPU check](#run-the-gpu-check)

## Current results and open work

| What runs | What was compared |
|---|---|
| **x64 programs from PE entry** | A two-record archive reader runs with blast 1.3 decompression under Windows, the PE mapper and the recompiled build. The three agree on output bytes, callback order, completed records, allocations, releases and exit status, including truncation and a refused output window. [Reproduce the archive comparison](docs/experiments.md#recompiling-the-blast-decoder) |
| **Raster draw from PE entry** | The shim-startup EXE reuses one D3D12 texture across three 64×64 draws, including a partial compute update and a pipeline change. Native, mapped and recompiled runs match all 16,384 RGBA bytes per frame. A skipped update is detected at the first stale pixel. [Reproduce the draw comparison](docs/experiments.md#exe-startup-through-the-desktop-runtime-shims) |
| **Pixel shaders** | At `c849f7a`, 851 of 12,101 PS records compiled, built D3D12 pipelines and matched controlled output on RTX 4060 Laptop and WARP. A two-mip draw verifies explicit LOD 0. A separate probe follows a constant-buffer read shared by 529 blocked records. Swapping buffers changes all 1,024 probe pixels. repos.desc: Windows shell replacement in Rust: taskbar, file manager, NTFS search, task manager, disk cleaner. One installer exe.
repos.readme:
# WinRust

**A Windows shell written in Rust: faster and lighter than the stock one.** Small native programs (no .NET, no Electron) that replace parts of Windows: the taskbar, File Explorer, file search, Task Manager, plus a disk cleaner, a disk map and a photo viewer. One installer puts them in, one button takes them all out.

English | [Русский](README.ru.md) | [日本語](README.ja.md) | [Português (Brasil)](README.pt-BR.md)

> **Read this first.** WinRust turns off Windows Search, hides the taskbar and can turn off Explorer as the shell. The exe is not code-signed, so SmartScreen will warn you. A restore point is created before install, but try it on a spare machine or a VM first.

## Install

1. Download `WinRust.exe` from the [latest release](https://github.com/Lemxy/WinRust/releases/latest) (Windows 10/11, x64).
2. Run it as administrator.
3. Tick the components you want and press the install button. On a fresh install, `rust-explorer` is unchecked. Tick it to replace the Windows Explorer shell (or use the gear on the topbar row: the **Shell: rust-explorer** switch). They are installed in the right order; one that fails or is skipped does not stop the others, the window lists what went wrong.

Windows Search is optional: on a stripped Windows (for example a debloated LTSC image without the Windows Search service) that step is skipped with a warning instead of failing the install.

If UAC asks for **another administrator's** password, the per-user settings (startup entries, scheduled tasks, PowerShell profile, search permissions) still go to the user who is signed in, not to the administrator you typed. If the installer cannot tell who that is, it stops before changing anything.

**Automatic updates:** after the first install, a `WinRust-update` scheduled task (runs as SYSTEM, no UAC prompt) checks the latest release at boot and once a day. It downloads only the programs that changed, checks each file against a manifest signed with the project's key (a tampered or unsigned release is refused) and replaces only files that are already installed. A running program switches to the new version the next time it starts (sign-in or reboot). Log: `%ProgramData%\plugin-la

repos.desc: Steer ideas like a space pilot!
repos.readme:
# 🕹️ Spaceship IDE

Steer ideas like a space pilot!

![Screencast](./extra/screencast.gif)

## Demos

Watch on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reels/DfyQPhFtW-z/) and [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3WmNLWUmcnY). You can try the simulator at [https://chuanqisun.github.io/spaceship/](https://chuanqisun.github.io/spaceship/) with the option to go live with your API keys for Cerebras and Gemini. Keys stay in your browser local storage. Do it at your own risk.

## Conjecture

> In the near future, LLM and Decision Models will reach 60 FPS interactivity.

When that happens, what new interaction paradigms will unlock? This project demonstrates plausible and desirable interactions for that future.

1. **Focus monitor**: can we visualize what LLM is paying attention to, and use that to guide human's focus towards what's important?

   ![focus monitor](./extra/clips/focus-monitor.gif)

2. **Attention lock**: can we force LLM to pay more attention to specific phrases so as to bias its future behavior?

   ![attention lock](./extra/clips/attention-lock.gif)

3. **Future Vector Steering**: can we decompose the task into eigenvectors, independently tune each, and re-compose them to influence the incoming text?

   ![future steering](./extra/clips/future-steering.gif)

4. **Realtime re-generation**: when text generation is cheap and fast, can we explore alternative futures by scrubbing?

   ![realtime regeneration](./extra/clips/realtime-regeneration.gif)

## Design process

I used Claude Code for most of the implementation but stayed hands-on for the UI/UX. I iterate using interactive style swatch, a technique where I prompt AI to give me diverse options of designs, I provide feedback, and it iterates. You can see the design artifacts in the [extra page](https://chuanqisun.github.io/spaceship/extra/style-1.html).

To achieve the realtime experience, I have to use agreesive speculative generation and manage cache invalidation based on user interactions. For example, when the main knob moves backward, I have to empty future texts and cancel ongoing requests. There are many considerations like this throughout the system and that took a lot of human judgement -
